initial_assessment: 34-year-old male presenting with approximately one week of headache and vomiting, consistent with raised intracranial pressure, and ECOG performance status 2. Brain MRI (2026-10-17) shows a well-circumscribed, lobulated, extra-axial/cortically based left frontal mass measuring 4.2 x 3.5 x 3.0 cm. Whole-spine MRI the same day shows a discrete, intensely and uniformly enhancing 5 mm lobulated nodule on the posterior pial surface of the cervical cord at C6, which is imaging-suspicious for spinal (drop) dissemination but is not biopsy-confirmed. A stereotactic needle biopsy of the left frontal mass was performed on 2026-10-19; the pathology report states only that findings are 'suggestive of an intracranial mesenchymal tumor with spinal drop metastasis' and explicitly note that the final histologic and molecular entity is NOT established on the current material. Correspondingly, the Condition resources for both the frontal mass (D43.0) and the C6 nodule (D43.4) are coded verificationStatus 'provisional', not confirmed. Working impression: a provisional intracranial mesenchymal neoplasm of uncertain behavior, entity and grade undetermined, with suspected but unconfirmed leptomeningeal/spinal dissemination. This is NOT a confirmed diagnosis; no specific CNS mesenchymal subtype (e.g., solitary fibrous tumor, sarcoma subtypes) should be assumed.
diagnostic_confirmation_and_staging: Priority is diagnostic confirmation. 1) Neuropathology review: arrange expert (reference/second-opinion) neuropathology review of the available stereotactic biopsy specimen, with a full immunohistochemistry workup appropriate to a mesenchymal differential (e.g., STAT6, CD34, S100/SOX10, EMA, SMA, desmin, myogenin, GFAP/OLIG2, reticulin, Ki-67 proliferative index) to narrow the entity. 2) Molecular workup: the biopsy material should undergo comprehensive molecular testing, including DNA methylation profiling/classification and GAP-complex next-generation sequencing covering gene fusions relevant to CNS mesenchymal tumors (e.g., FGFR1/2/3, NTRK/ETV6, BRAF, CIC, BCOR, MYB-related and other rearrangements). These results are the key determinants of whether a defined, potentially actionable entity emerges. 3) Adequacy of tissue: assess whether the stereotactic biopsy yielded sufficient representative tissue; if material is inadequate or results remain indeterminate, discuss obtaining additional tissue (repeat biopsy vs. maximal safe resection of the accessible left frontal lesion) at the multidisciplinary board. 4) Confirm the nature of the C6 pial nodule: it is imaging-suspicious but unproven - plan CSF cytology (only when intracranial pressure status has been assessed and lumbar puncture is deemed safe) and/or discuss tissue sampling, and re-image to assess evolution. 5) Complete safe staging: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (or whole-body FDG-PET/CT) to exclude a systemic primary or systemic metastatic disease, fundoscopy for papilledema, and formal neurosurgical evaluation of resectability of the frontal mass. Multi-planar review by neuroradiology of both MRI studies to characterize the mass fully (dural attachment, edema, midline shift, hydrocephalus) is warranted.
immediate_management_plan: Short-horizon plan focused on diagnosis, safety and symptom control: 1) Symptom control: start and titrate dexamethasone for suspected raised intracranial pressure/vasogenic edema with a predefined taper goal, co-prescribe gastric (PPI) protection, and monitor glycemia. Avoid delaying or empirically curtailing steroids without discussion with pathology, recognizing steroids may obscure tissue yields for differential diagnoses other than the suggested mesenchymal process. 2) Neurologic monitoring: serial neurologic assessments; urgent imaging if deterioration. Evaluate hydrocephalus/mass effect before any consideration of lumbar puncture; anticonvulsant therapy only for clinical indication, not routinely. 3) Multidisciplinary review: convene the neuro-oncology tumor board (neurosurgery, neuropathology, neuroradiology, radiation oncology, medical neuro-oncology) with all imaging and the biopsy material; plan expedited molecular testing turnaround. 4) Disease-directed therapy (definitive surgery vs. biopsy-based management, chemotherapy, radiotherapy) is DEFERRED until the histologic/molecular entity, WHO grade, extent of dissemination, and resectability are established; with an unspecified intracranial mesenchymal tumor and currently insufficient molecular information, no definitive regimen can or should be constructed. 5) Supportive care: patient and family education emphasizing diagnostic uncertainty, analgesia for headache, antiemetics, baseline antineoplastic-treatment workup (blood counts, chemistries, renal/hepatic function) so the patient is treatment-ready if a regimen is later justified, and early palliative-care/supportive involvement. This plan should be revisited as soon as molecular/pathology results arrive.
prognosis: Prognosis cannot be usefully quantified at this stage and quoting a survival figure before diagnosis is confirmed would be misleading. It depends on: (1) the final histologic and molecular ENTITY within the intracranial mesenchymal tumor differential, which spans a wide spectrum of behavior; (2) the WHO CNS GRADE assigned once the entity is established; (3) the EXTENT of disease - specifically whether the C6 pial nodule is confirmed as true neuraxis dissemination, which would stage the disease as leptomeningeal/spinal spread and worsen outlook for most candidate entities; (4) RESECTABILITY and achievable extent of resection of the frontal mass and any spinal disease; and (5) the presence or absence of actionable molecular alterations, which could open targeted-therapy options. Once entity and grade are confirmed, a more precise prognosis can be given.
